query: Equiatomic HfNbTaTiZr exhibits 8–16% room-temperature tensile ductility in the cast state and a yield strength of 163–530 MPa at 1000 °C at strain rates of 10−4–10−2 s−1, but inadequate oxygen resistance prevents most practical high-temperature applications. Earlier oxidation-protection research prevented pesting in a related, non-equiatomic Hf–Nb–Ta–Ti–Zr alloy during a 5 h exposure to air at 800 °C, but that result does not establish protection for equiatomic HfNbTaTiZr; related studies on other refractory alloys likewise did not evaluate this composition. With preservation of useful room- and high-temperature mechanical performance as a design constraint, what single intervention could improve the oxygen resistance of equiatomic cast HfNbTaTiZr? Formulate one hypothesis identifying the intervention and mechanism, predicting the outcome relative to untreated material, defining the applicable temperature, atmosphere, exposure-time, and loading boundaries, citing supporting evidence from the prior studies, and specifying a controlled experiment and result that would falsify the hypothesis.

generation.hypothesis: Adding a minor amount of aluminum (around 5 atomic percent) to equiatomic cast HfNbTaTiZr will improve its oxygen resistance by encouraging the formation of a thin, adherent Al2O3 layer, while preserving its beneficial room- and high-temperature mechanical properties.
generation.material_initial_state: Equiatomic cast HfNbTaTiZr that shows 8–16% room-temperature tensile ductility and a yield strength of 163–530 MPa at 1000 °C but suffers from rapid oxidation (pesting) due to inadequate oxygen resistance.
generation.intervention: Introduce approximately 5 at.% aluminum into the HfNbTaTiZr alloy composition during casting.
generation.conditions: Oxidation tests in air at 800 °C for a duration of 5 hours under static or low-strain conditions; subsequent mechanical testing at room temperature and 1000 °C under comparable strain rates (10^−4–10^−2 s^−1) as in previous studies.
generation.structural_mediator: The formation of a continuous, slow-growing, and adherent alumina (Al2O3) scale on the alloy surface.
generation.mechanism: Aluminum has a high oxygen affinity and, when present, will preferentially oxidize to form a robust Al2O3 film. This protective scale acts as a barrier against further oxygen ingress, thereby reducing the oxidation rate (pesting behavior) without significantly altering the bulk microstructure that governs the mechanical performance.
generation.predicted_outcome: The modified alloy should exhibit a significantly lower oxidation weight gain and avoid pesting (i.e., the oxide scale remains adherent and continuous) relative to untreated equiatomic HfNbTaTiZr, while retaining its room-temperature ductility and high-temperature yield strength.
generation.baseline: Untreated equiatomic HfNbTaTiZr, which under air exposure at 800 °C for 5 hours shows rapid oxidation and degradation (pesting) despite having acceptable mechanical performance.
generation.boundary: The beneficial effects are expected to hold under conditions close to 800 °C in air for at least 5 hours and under the same strain-rate and loading conditions as previously characterized; deviation outside these ranges may require further evaluation.
generation.uncertainty: The optimal aluminum content to balance improved oxidation resistance with preservation of the mechanical properties is uncertain; while 5 at.% is a reasonable starting point based on analogous studies, fine tuning may be necessary. Additionally, the long-term stability and scalability of the protective alumina layer under cyclic loading or thermal cycling need further confirmation.

falsification_experiment.design: Synthesize two sets of alloys: one set of standard equiatomic HfNbTaTiZr and another set with approximately 5 at.% aluminum added. Subject both sets to air exposure at 800 °C for 5 hours under identical loading (or no load) conditions. Subsequently, characterize the surface oxide scales using SEM and measure oxidation weight gain. Perform tensile tests at room temperature and at 1000 °C (at strain rates of 10^−4–10^−2 s^−1) to evaluate any changes in ductility and yield strength.
measurements: Oxidation weight gain measurements and oxide-layer morphology (e.g., via SEM)
Adherence and integrity of the oxide scale (e.g., through spallation tests)
Tensile mechanical properties at room temperature and at 1000 °C (ductility and yield strength)
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the aluminum-added alloy does not exhibit a statistically significant improvement in oxidation resistance (i.e., similar or higher oxidation weight gain, spallation, or poor oxide adherence) or if its mechanical properties (room-temperature ductility and high-temperature yield strength) are compromised beyond acceptable limits compared to the untreated alloy, then the hypothesis is falsified.

cited_evidence.text: Refractory high-entropy alloys (RHEAs) are considered to be a new generation of high-temperature materials, because they have the advantages of both high-entropy alloys (HEAs) and refractory metals (RMs), such as high-temperature strength, high hardness, and good phase stability at high temperatures [ [1] , [2] , [3] , [4] , [5] , [6] , [7] ]. They are mainly composed of Mo, Nb, Ta, and W, while Ti, Cr, V, Si, and Al are usually used as strengthening alloy elements [ [8] , [9] , [10] , [11] , [12] , [13] , [14] ]. For example, Mo 25 Nb 25 Ta 25 W 25 and Mo 20 Nb 20 Ta 20 W 20 V 20 are two of the types of most extensively studied RHEAs [ [7] ]. The neutron diffraction analysis of those alloys after annealing at 1400 °C for 19 h shows that no changes have occurred to their phase structures. Their compression yield strengths are much higher than that of Inconel 718 alloy at temperatures above 800 °C. Furthermore, their yield strengths are still higher than 500 MPa at 1200 °C [ [15] , [16] ].
